title: SYSK Selects: Geysers: Nature's Innuendo
summary: SYSK Selects rerun of the 2012 episode "Geysers: Nature's Innuendo." Josh and Chuck explain how geysers work: a water supply from precipitation percolating through the crust, a plumbing system of fissures sealed with rhyolite silica, and a heat source from shallow volcanic or magmatic activity. Pressure builds because the water cannot boil, like a pressure cooker, until it flashes to steam and erupts. They distinguish geysers from hot springs, describe cone versus fountain geysers (Old Faithful, Grand Geyser, Wymani/Waimangu), discuss the 1903 Waimangu deaths in New Zealand, threats from geothermal energy production and mineral extraction, and the Strokkur geyser in Iceland. The episode closes with a Prince anecdote and a listener mail about labor unions, a New York City union organizer, the Triangle Shirtwaist fire, and a Brooklyn City Council candidate's campaign plug.

segments.title: Opening banter and rerun introduction
segments.summary: Josh introduces this SYSK Select, a 2012 episode on geysers. The hosts joke about common geyser myths and tease the episode, and mention a 1903 New Zealand geyser incident.

segments.title: Geyser basics and 1903 deaths
segments.summary: The hosts say geysers are fragile and rare, with about a thousand worldwide and roughly fifty geyser fields, and that Yellowstone has many. Geysers relate to hot springs, fumaroles, mud pots and steam vents, all driven by shallow geothermal activity. They note the 1903 deaths of four tourists at Wairingi/Wymani valley in New Zealand.

segments.title: Water supply, plumbing and heat source
segments.summary: A geyser needs three components: a water supply, a plumbing system, and a heat source. Water is mainly precipitation that percolates through the crust over thousands of years until it meets shallow hot rock or young volcanic activity.

segments.title: Rhyolite-sealed plumbing and pressure
segments.summary: The plumbing consists of fissures miles beneath the surface sealed with silica from rhyolite, which makes them watertight. Geysers differ from hot springs because an obstruction or the weight of deep water creates a bottleneck and pressure.

segments.title: Pressure cooker boiling point and eruption
segments.summary: Using a pressure cooker analogy, the hosts explain that pressure raises the boiling point. Superheated water is released when pressure drops, and it flashes to steam that expands greatly, producing the eruption. The cycle repeats as the geyser refills.

segments.title: Old Faithful eruption timing and famous geysers
segments.summary: Old Faithful erupts on a roughly bimodal schedule, with long eruptions over four minutes or short ones about two and a half minutes. Cone geysers like Old Faithful differ from fountain geysers like Grand Geyser, the tallest regularly erupting geyser. Other geysers mentioned include Stroker, Steamboat, Wymani and Geysir.

segments.title: Threats to geysers and the Strokkur revival
segments.summary: The hosts discuss geothermal energy production and mineral extraction, which can harm geysers, and the earthquakes that can shut them off or revive them. Stroker, in Iceland, went dormant after earthquakes and was later cleared and reactivated.

segments.title: Prince and sign-off
segments.summary: Brief tangents and sign-off, including a Prince anecdote, and the closing note that the geyser article is searchable on the site.
